locations.name: Damascus
locations.period: Iron Age, with occupation continuing through later periods
locations.description: Damascus was the political center of Aram-Damascus and one of the principal urban centers of the southern Levant. Much of the ancient city lies beneath the modern city, so the archaeological record is unevenly accessible. Its association with Aram-Damascus is supported by historical and epigraphic evidence; the material record should not be used to assume a single uniform population.

site.period_studied: Iron Age, with occupation continuing through later periods
site.research_focus: Urban stratigraphy, fortifications, architecture, inscriptions, and changing city organization
site.excavation_history: Archaeological work in Damascus has taken place through excavations, surveys, and architectural investigations in areas accessible around the modern city. The ancient settlement cannot be represented by one continuous excavation campaign because modern occupation limits access to many areas.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a complete campaign and director list for Damascus; this fieldwork entry should be expanded when project-level sources are added.
site.description: Damascus was the political center of Aram-Damascus and one of the principal urban centers of the southern Levant. Archaeological work is constrained because much of the ancient city lies beneath the modern city, making the surviving record unevenly accessible.
site.historical_significance: Damascus is central to the history of Aram-Damascus, but its archaeological record reflects successive periods and populations. The city should not be treated as evidence for one uniform identity across its entire history.
site.major_findings: Accessible investigations document urban architecture, fortifications, inscriptions, and material remains connected with the long history of the city. The evidence is spatially uneven and should be combined with historical and epigraphic sources.

locations.name: Hama
locations.period: Iron Age, especially the 12th-8th centuries BC
locations.description: Hama, ancient Hamath, was a long-lived urban center on the Orontes River. The kingdom of Hamath included Luwian and Aramaic cultural and linguistic elements, and its inscriptions reflect that complex history. It is more accurate to describe Hama as an urban center associated with Hamath than to assign the entire site to one uniform identity.

site.period_studied: Bronze Age through Iron Age and later occupation
site.research_focus: Settlement sequence, urban development, inscriptions, and regional exchange
site.excavation_history: The principal early excavation was the Danish Archaeological Expedition to Hama, conducted from 1931 to 1938. The work was directed by Harald Ingholt and produced a stratified record that remains important for the chronology of western Syria; later research has continued through the study of the expedition archives and finds.
site.excavation_team: The main historical fieldwork was carried out by the Danish Archaeological Expedition under Harald Ingholt, supported by archaeologists, architects, surveyors, and specialists responsible for ceramics, inscriptions, and artefact analysis.
site.description: The Hama mound preserves a long occupational sequence in the Orontes valley. Excavated levels document changing settlement forms, ceramics, architecture, administrative activity, and written evidence from the Bronze Age through the Iron Age and later periods. The site’s evidence reflects a region where Luwian, Aramaic, and other traditions interacted.
site.historical_significance: Hama is valuable because it connects a long-lived urban mound with the political history of Hamath and the wider Orontes valley. Its evidence supports historical reconstruction, but the site cannot be reduced to one language, dynasty, or ethnic identity across all periods.
site.major_findings: The excavations established a sequence from early settlement through the Bronze and Iron Ages and later occupation. They recovered urban architecture, ceramics, inscriptions, and cuneiform tablets, including evidence relevant to administration, religion, and regional exchange.

locations.name: Tell Halaf
locations.description: Guzana, identified with Tell Halaf, was the principal center of Bit-Bahiani. The site is known for its monumental palace, basalt sculptures, orthostats, and evidence of a complex urban tradition in the Khabur region. These remains document a political and artistic setting without making material culture a simple ethnic marker.

site.research_focus: Palace architecture, sculptures, orthostats, and urban organization
site.excavation_history: Max von Oppenheim identified the site in 1899 and directed major German excavations in 1911-1913 and again in 1927-1929. The finds were later studied, reconstructed, and divided between museum collections; more recent scholarship has reassessed the architecture, sculptures, and earlier occupation in their archaeological contexts.
site.excavation_team: The first major campaigns were led by Max von Oppenheim with a German archaeological team. The excavation, conservation, reconstruction, and later study involved specialists in architecture, sculpture, epigraphy, and ancient Near Eastern archaeology.
site.description: The Tell Halaf mound preserves a long sequence of occupation, including the prehistoric tradition later called Halaf and the Iron Age center identified with Guzana. The Iron Age remains include monumental buildings, carved basalt sculpture, orthostats, and evidence for an organized urban and political center in the Khabur region.
site.historical_significance: The remains show how a northern Mesopotamian center developed across different periods. The palace and sculpture are important evidence for political representation and regional interaction, but material style alone does not establish a single continuous ethnic identity.
site.major_findings: The excavations documented an Iron Age palace complex, carved basalt orthostats and sculptures, urban buildings, and material connected with Guzana and Bit-Bahiani. They also established the importance of the site for the study of the prehistoric Halaf tradition, although the prehistoric and Iron Age phases must not be conflated.

locations.name: Zincirli
locations.description: Sam’al, excavated at Zincirli, was a fortified urban center ruled by the Bit-Gabbar dynasty. Its citadel, gates, sculptures, and inscriptions provide rich evidence for local kingship, administration, language, and religious practice. The site also shows interaction among Aramean, Luwian, Phoenician, and Assyrian traditions.

site.period_studied: Iron Age occupation, with earlier Bronze Age settlement
site.research_focus: Citadel, gates, palaces, sculptures, inscriptions, and city planning
site.excavation_history: The first major campaigns took place between 1888 and 1902. A German expedition worked on behalf of the German Orient-Comité and the Berlin Museum; Carl Humann participated in the first campaign, followed by Felix von Luschan and Robert Koldewey. The Chicago-Tübingen Expedition later resumed fieldwork and continues to study the settlement and its regional setting.
site.excavation_team: The historical excavations were conducted by German teams led successively by Carl Humann, Felix von Luschan, and Robert Koldewey. Modern research is associated with the Chicago-Tübingen Expedition, a collaborative archaeological and interdisciplinary project.
site.description: Zincirli preserves a fortified settlement with a citadel, lower town, monumental gates, royal buildings, sculptures, and inscriptions. The site’s long sequence allows researchers to compare earlier settlement, Iron Age Sam’al, and the changing political conditions created by interaction with neighboring powers and later Assyrian administration.
site.historical_significance: Sam’al is a major case study for the interaction of Aramean, Luwian, Phoenician, and Assyrian political and cultural traditions. The city’s material record should be read as a changing historical sequence rather than as evidence of one uniform population or cultural system.
site.major_findings: Fieldwork exposed the double fortification system, gates, palatial and administrative buildings, sculptures, inscriptions, and the lower town. Modern excavations have also identified earlier Bronze Age settlement beneath parts of the Iron Age town and have recovered important evidence such as the Katumuwa funerary stele.

locations.name: Tell Ahmar
locations.description: Til Barsip, identified with Tell Ahmar, was the capital of Bit-Adini on the Euphrates. The settlement continued under Assyrian control, so its remains reflect changing political administrations rather than one period. Its urban and palatial evidence is important for studying interaction between Aramean and Assyrian institutions.

site.period_studied: Iron Age and Assyrian-period occupation, with earlier settlement
site.research_focus: Palace architecture, wall paintings, inscriptions, and changing administration
site.excavation_history: A French expedition excavated the site from 1929 to 1931 under François Thureau-Dangin. Rescue and renewed archaeological work has also been associated with Guy Bunnens and the University of Melbourne since the late twentieth century, while later scholarship continues to reassess the earlier excavation records and assemblages.
site.excavation_team: The first major excavation was directed by François Thureau-Dangin with a French archaeological team. Later Australian-led work associated with Guy Bunnens expanded the study of the settlement, its stratigraphy, and its material culture.
site.description: Tell Ahmar occupies a strategic position on the Euphrates and is associated with Til Barsip, also known in other periods by related names. Excavated remains include an Iron Age urban center, palatial architecture, wall paintings, inscriptions, administrative structures, and evidence for the transformation of local institutions under Assyrian rule.
site.historical_significance: Til Barsip is especially useful for studying political change along the Euphrates, from local and regional rule to Assyrian provincial administration. The site’s names and political affiliations changed over time, so the archaeological record should not be treated as evidence for one unchanging polity.
site.major_findings: The excavations documented the palace and urban center, painted wall decoration, inscriptions, fortifications, and later Assyrian administrative phases. Earlier occupation and funerary contexts show that the mound’s history began before the Iron Age and continued through successive political administrations.

locations.name: Tell Tayinat
locations.description: Kunulua, identified with Tell Tayinat, was the capital of Pattin/Unqi in the Amuq plain. The site preserves evidence for a kingdom shaped by Neo-Hittite and Aramean traditions. It should be studied as a politically and culturally mixed urban center rather than assigned to one identity solely from its material remains.

site.period_studied: Iron Age occupation, with earlier and later settlement
site.research_focus: Palace and temple architecture, administration, and Neo-Hittite-Aramean interaction
site.excavation_history: Large-scale excavations were conducted in 1935-1938, and the Tayinat Archaeological Project resumed systematic fieldwork in 2004. The modern project has combined excavation with survey, conservation, epigraphy, archaeobotany, and other specialist studies.
site.excavation_team: The modern Tayinat Archaeological Project has been directed for many years by Timothy Harrison of the University of Toronto, with assistant directors, field archaeologists, epigraphers, conservators, and environmental and artefact specialists. Earlier work was conducted by a University of Chicago/Oriental Institute expedition.
site.description: Tell Tayinat is a major settlement in the Amuq plain, commonly associated with Kunulua, the center of the Iron Age kingdom of Patina/Unqi. Excavations have documented monumental architecture, administrative spaces, temples, inscriptions, and evidence for later Neo-Assyrian provincial control.
site.historical_significance: The site is important for tracing interaction among local Iron Age kingdoms, Anatolian and Levantine traditions, and the Neo-Assyrian provincial system. The identification of Tell Tayinat with Kunulua is widely used but remains an archaeological and historical reconstruction based on the evidence.
site.major_findings: Excavations have exposed a monumental citadel gate, palace and temple buildings, administrative contexts, inscriptions, and a Neo-Assyrian temple. The 2008-2009 seasons also recovered burned cultic objects and eleven cuneiform tablets or fragments from the temple’s inner sanctum.

locations.name: Bahadirli
locations.modern_location: Bahadirli, near Karatepe, Osmaniye Province, Turkey
locations.associated_context: Aramaic boundary inscription and the cult of Kubaba
locations.description: Bahadirli is the reported findspot of an eight-line Aramaic boundary inscription discovered about 6 km north of Karatepe in Cilicia. The stone is associated with the territorial boundary of KRBYL and KRŠY and invokes Kubaba of PWŠD/R, but the ancient place-name identifications remain interpretive.

locations.name: Tell Afis
locations.description: Hazrek, commonly associated with Tell Afis, was the center of Lu’ash and was later connected politically with Hamath under King Zakkur. The site and the Zakkur inscription are important for reconstructing political networks in northern Syria, although the relationship between a named polity and every archaeological layer must be assessed separately.

site.period_studied: Late Chalcolithic through Iron Age occupation
site.research_focus: Urban settlement, regional political networks, and the Lu’ash context
site.excavation_history: The site has been investigated through several campaigns and surveys, including a long-running Italian-led excavation project associated with Stefania Mazzoni. Later conservation, rescue, and museum work also involved University of Florence specialists, including Candida Felli, especially after the interruption and damage affecting archaeological work in Syria.
site.excavation_team: The principal modern project has been directed by Stefania Mazzoni with Italian and Syrian collaboration. Field archaeologists, ceramic specialists, epigraphers, architects, and conservation teams have contributed to the excavation and study of the mound.
site.description: Tell Afis is a large multi-period mound whose occupation extends from the fourth millennium into the first millennium BC. Its Iron Age remains include an acropolis, temples, fortifications, domestic and administrative areas, and artefacts that help reconstruct the political and economic networks of northern Syria.
site.historical_significance: Tell Afis provides evidence for changing urban and political organization in northern Syria. Its association with named Iron Age places is reconstructed through the combined use of archaeology, inscriptions, and regional comparison, so individual identifications remain interpretive rather than automatic.
site.major_findings: Work has revealed a long urban sequence, Iron Age temple and settlement remains, fortifications, and artefacts from the acropolis. The site is also studied in relation to Hazrek and Lu’ash and to the wider historical setting in which the Zakkur Stele was produced; the stele should not be presented as a find made by the modern excavation team at Tell Afis.

locations.name: Tell Rifaat
locations.description: Arpad, commonly identified with Tell Rifaat, was the capital of Bit-Agusi. Its political importance is also reflected in the Sefire treaty stelae, which record diplomatic relations involving the kingdom. The identification of ancient political territory with the full extent of the archaeological settlement remains an interpretive reconstruction.

site.research_focus: Urban settlement, fortifications, political organization, and regional networks
site.excavation_history: Archaeological investigations and surveys at Tell Rifaat have examined the mound, its settlement sequence, and regional setting. A complete campaign chronology is not yet recorded in this catalogue and requires additional project-level source documentation.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a complete list of excavation directors or institutions for Tell Rifaat; this information remains to be added from dedicated fieldwork sources.
site.description: Arpad, commonly identified with Tell Rifaat, was the capital of Bit-Agusi. The identification connects the archaeological mound with a major Iron Age polity, but the extent of the ancient political territory remains a historical reconstruction.
site.historical_significance: Arpad is important for reconstructing Iron Age political organization in northern Syria. The identification of Tell Rifaat with ancient Arpad is presented as an interpretation rather than as an automatic equivalence between every layer and the named kingdom.
site.major_findings: The site preserves urban and defensive remains relevant to the study of northern Syrian settlement and the political networks associated with Bit-Agusi. The Sefire treaty stelae are related evidence for the polity but are not treated as finds from Tell Rifaat itself.

locations.name: Şanlıurfa
locations.period: 1st century BC-3rd century AD, especially the Osroene period
locations.description: Urhay, known in Greek and Latin sources as Edessa, was the capital of Osroene and a major center of Aramaic and later Syriac cultural production. Its inscriptions, mosaics, and funerary remains document urban life in the Roman-period Near East. This later urban history should be distinguished from the Iron Age kingdoms in the catalogue.

site.period_studied: 1st century BC-3rd century AD, especially the Osroene period
site.research_focus: Urban archaeology, inscriptions, mosaics, tombs, and the development of Aramaic and Syriac communities
site.excavation_history: Archaeological work at and around Şanlıurfa has documented urban, religious, and funerary contexts from the ancient city. Because the modern city overlies much of ancient Edessa, the record combines excavations, rescue work, architectural study, and material evidence from different contexts.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a consolidated history of the excavation teams and urban archaeology projects at Edessa; project-specific documentation remains to be added.
site.description: Urhay, known in Greek and Latin sources as Edessa, was the capital of Osroene and a major center of Aramaic and later Syriac cultural production. Its archaeological record is distributed across a modern urban environment and includes inscriptions, mosaics, and funerary remains.
site.historical_significance: Urhay is important for the archaeology of later Aramaic-speaking urban communities and the development of Syriac culture. Its later history must be distinguished from the Iron Age kingdoms represented elsewhere in the catalogue.
site.major_findings: Investigated contexts include inscriptions, mosaics, tombs, architectural remains, and evidence for later Christian and Syriac communities. These findings represent different periods and should not be collapsed into a single archaeological phase.

locations.name: Palmyra
locations.associated_context: Palmyrene Aramaic and Roman-period civic culture
locations.description: Palmyra was a major oasis city whose inscriptions document Palmyrene Aramaic, civic institutions, trade, and religious life. Its archaeology reflects a multilingual and interconnected urban society; Palmyrene evidence should not be treated as identical to the Iron Age kingdoms of Aram.

site.research_focus: Urban planning, temples, inscriptions, civic institutions, trade, and funerary architecture
site.excavation_history: Excavations, surveys, and conservation projects at Palmyra have investigated the city, its temples, colonnaded streets, domestic areas, and funerary landscapes. The record includes work from different periods and institutions and should be organized through project-specific sources.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a complete list of the Syrian and international excavation and conservation projects at Palmyra; that research history remains to be documented separately.
site.description: Palmyra was a major oasis city whose inscriptions document Palmyrene Aramaic, civic institutions, trade, and religious life. Its archaeology reflects a multilingual and interconnected urban society rather than a single uniform cultural system.
site.historical_significance: Palmyra is essential for studying later Aramaic language and culture in a cosmopolitan urban setting. Its evidence belongs to a later period than the Iron Age Aramean kingdoms and should be interpreted within its Palmyrene and Roman contexts.
site.major_findings: Fieldwork has documented monumental temples, civic architecture, streets, houses, tombs, sculptures, and extensive Palmyrene Aramaic inscriptions. These remains provide evidence for civic, religious, commercial, and family life in the Roman-period city.

locations.name: Hatra
locations.associated_context: Hatran Aramaic and the Hatran kingdom
locations.description: Hatra was a fortified city and religious center whose inscriptions are written in Hatran Aramaic. Its monumental sanctuaries and civic buildings document a later Mesopotamian urban tradition and should be distinguished chronologically from the Iron Age Aramean polities.

site.research_focus: Fortifications, sanctuaries, civic buildings, sculpture, and Hatran Aramaic inscriptions
site.excavation_history: Archaeological excavations and conservation work at Hatra have examined the fortified city, major sanctuaries, civic buildings, sculptures, and inscriptions. The catalogue requires additional project-level documentation before a complete campaign history can be stated.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a complete institutional and director history for the Hatra excavations; this field should be expanded from dedicated archaeological sources.
site.description: Hatra was a fortified city and religious center whose inscriptions are written in Hatran Aramaic. Its monumental sanctuaries and civic buildings document a later Mesopotamian urban tradition distinct from the Iron Age Aramean polities.
site.historical_significance: Hatra is important for the study of a later Aramaic-speaking urban kingdom and for the relationship between local religious traditions and wider Mesopotamian political systems.
site.major_findings: Investigated remains include the city walls, monumental sanctuaries, civic architecture, sculpture, and a large corpus of Hatran Aramaic inscriptions. The evidence documents urban and religious life in the Parthian-period northern Mesopotamian context.

locations.name: Dura-Europos
locations.description: Dura-Europos was a fortified city on the Euphrates with Parthian and Roman phases. Its inscriptions, documents, religious buildings, and domestic remains show how Aramaic functioned within a multilingual frontier community.

site.research_focus: Fortifications, temples, churches, houses, documents, and funerary contexts
site.excavation_history: Franz Cumont conducted the first major excavations for the French Academy in 1922-1924 and 1926-1927. Yale University joined the project in 1928, and major Yale and French campaigns continued through 1937, with Michael Rostovtzeff playing a central role in the Yale expedition and its publications.
site.excavation_team: The early work was led by Franz Cumont and a French team. The later large-scale campaigns were a collaboration between Yale University and the French Academy, involving Michael Rostovtzeff and specialists in architecture, inscriptions, art history, conservation, and ancient documents.
site.description: Dura-Europos was a fortified city on the Euphrates whose excavated remains preserve civic, military, domestic, religious, and funerary contexts. The city’s inscriptions, documents, paintings, and architecture show how Greek, Roman, Iranian, and local Semitic traditions operated within a changing frontier settlement.
site.historical_significance: Dura-Europos is a comparative site for studying religious plurality, administration, military life, and language use in a frontier city. Its evidence documents coexistence and interaction among communities, but it should not be used to imply that all inhabitants shared one identity or language.
site.major_findings: Excavations uncovered city walls, houses, military buildings, temples, the Mithraeum, a synagogue with painted biblical scenes, and one of the earliest known Christian house churches. Written documents and graffiti in several languages provide unusually detailed evidence for the city’s institutions and communities.

locations.name: et-Tell
locations.period: Iron Age, especially the 10th-8th centuries BC
locations.description: Bethsaida, identified by many researchers with et-Tell, was a fortified settlement and regional center associated with Geshur. Its gate complex and cultic remains are important for studying settlement organization in the southern Levant. The association is an interpretation, not proof that every population at the site shared one identity.

site.research_focus: City gate, fortifications, cultic installations, and settlement organization
site.excavation_history: The Bethsaida Excavations Project began work at et-Tell in the late 1980s and has continued through successive seasons. The project has been directed by Rami Arav, first in association with the University of Haifa and later with the University of Nebraska at Omaha, together with an international field team.
site.excavation_team: The principal modern team is the Bethsaida Excavations Project led by Rami Arav. Archaeologists, surveyors, architects, ceramic specialists, and students have worked across the gate, fortification, public, cultic, and domestic areas.
site.description: The et-Tell mound contains substantial Iron Age architecture and later occupation. Excavated areas include fortifications, a city gate complex, a large public or administrative building, cultic installations, domestic areas, and remains from the Roman-period settlement. The identification of et-Tell with Bethsaida is influential but remains part of an ongoing archaeological discussion.
site.historical_significance: The site is important for examining settlement and kingship in the Golan and northern Jordan Valley. Because the identification with Bethsaida and the relationship to Geshur involve interpretation, the page distinguishes excavated remains from the historical labels applied to them.
site.major_findings: Fieldwork has exposed Iron Age city walls, a monumental gate and associated bastions, a possible high-place or cultic area, public architecture, and later Roman-period remains. A cultic stele and other objects contribute to the study of local religious practice, but they do not by themselves prove a single ethnic or political identity.

locations.name: Tell Fekheriye
locations.description: Tell Fekheriye was a settlement and administrative center in the orbit of Guzana. The bilingual statue of Hadad-yis’i found there is important evidence for the use of Assyrian and Aramaic in the same political environment. The inscription identifies an official and a context; it does not define the ethnicity of the entire settlement.

site.period_studied: Mittani and Assyrian periods, with earlier and later occupation
site.research_focus: Settlement sequence, administrative architecture, bilingual inscription, and cuneiform tablets
site.excavation_history: Exploratory work and smaller campaigns took place in 1929, 1940, and 1955. The famous bilingual statue and inscription are reported as having been discovered at the site in 1979. A joint German-Syrian project conducted intensive excavation campaigns from 2005 to 2010, including work on administrative buildings and associated artefacts.
site.excavation_team: The site has been investigated through several campaigns involving international and Syrian researchers. The 2005-2010 work is described as a joint German-Syrian project; the available record does not yet provide a complete list of directors or participating institutions.
site.description: Tell Fekheriye is a mound in the Khabur basin with evidence for settlement and administrative activity across multiple periods. Its archaeological record is especially important for the bilingual Hadad-yis'i statue and inscription and for the study of the political environment associated with Guzana and Bit-Bahiani.
site.historical_significance: Tell Fekheriye is important for reconstructing the relationship between Assyrian and Aramaic language use in the Khabur region and for studying the administrative setting associated with Guzana and Bit-Bahiani. The site evidence documents a political and linguistic environment without establishing a uniform identity for every period or population.
site.major_findings: Excavations and earlier investigations documented settlement remains, administrative architecture, ancient artefacts, and the bilingual royal statue and inscription of Hadad-yis'i. The mound has been associated in different hypotheses with ancient names such as Sikkan or Washshukanni, but those identifications remain interpretive and are not treated here as certain.

locations.name: Al-Nayrab
locations.classification: Village or local settlement and funerary context
locations.description: Neirab, near Aleppo, is known archaeologically through two funerary stelae with Aramaic inscriptions and representations of priests. The evidence is valuable for studying local religious and funerary practice, but it does not establish a separate kingdom or a single identity for the whole community.

site.research_focus: Funerary contexts, local religious practice, and Aramaic inscriptions
site.excavation_history: Investigations at Neirab have focused on the funerary contexts and inscriptional evidence associated with the settlement. The current catalogue does not yet contain a complete campaign history or fieldwork bibliography.
site.excavation_team: The excavation and recovery history of the Neirab funerary material requires additional source documentation before individual teams can be identified here.
site.description: Neirab, near Aleppo, is known archaeologically through funerary stelae with Aramaic inscriptions and representations of priests. The site is included as a local settlement and funerary context, not as evidence for a separate kingdom.
site.historical_significance: Neirab is valuable for studying Aramaic funerary language and religious practice in northern Syria. Its evidence should not be expanded into a claim for a separate Neirab kingdom or uniform community identity.
site.major_findings: The principal archaeological evidence consists of funerary stelae, inscriptions, and representations connected with local religious practice. These remains illuminate a specific community and ritual context rather than a wider political territory.

locations.name: Ein Gev
locations.period: Iron Age, including the 9th century BC
locations.associated_context: Possible Aramean political presence; attribution remains cautious
locations.description: Ein Gev was a lakeside settlement on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee. An Aramaic inscription from the site has been used in discussions of Aramean administrative or political activity in the region. The inscription cannot by itself establish continuous Aramean control or a uniform population.

site.period_studied: Iron Age, including the 9th century BC
site.research_focus: Settlement organization, regional political presence, and Aramaic inscriptional evidence
site.excavation_history: Archaeological excavations and surveys at Ein Gev have investigated the settlement and its regional setting. The fieldwork record requires additional project-level sources for a complete campaign chronology and excavation history.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a consolidated list of the Ein Gev excavation teams and institutions; those details remain to be added from dedicated fieldwork sources.
site.description: Ein Gev was a lakeside settlement on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee. An Aramaic inscription from the site has been used in discussions of Aramean administrative or political activity, but it cannot by itself establish continuous control or a uniform population.
site.historical_significance: Ein Gev helps place Aramaic political and administrative evidence within the wider regional history of the Galilee and Golan. Its attribution remains cautious because the evidence is limited and belongs to a changing political landscape.
site.major_findings: Investigated contexts include settlement remains and inscriptional evidence relevant to the Iron Age eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee. The Aramaic inscription is treated as evidence for a historical discussion, not as proof of uninterrupted Aramean rule.

locations.name: Arslan Tash
locations.description: Arslan Tash, ancient Hadatu, was an important settlement in the Euphrates region and became an Assyrian provincial center after the defeat of Bit-Adini. Ivories, inscriptions, and other finds preserve evidence of changing political and administrative systems.

site.research_focus: Fortifications, palace architecture, ivories, inscriptions, and Assyrian provincial administration
site.excavation_history: Archaeological excavations and surveys at Arslan Tash have investigated the settlement, monumental architecture, ivories, inscriptions, and later provincial contexts. A complete campaign chronology and project bibliography remain to be added to this catalogue.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a consolidated record of the excavation directors and institutions at Arslan Tash; project-level source documentation is still required.
site.description: Arslan Tash, ancient Hadatu, was an important settlement in the Euphrates region and became an Assyrian provincial center after the defeat of Bit-Adini. Its material record preserves evidence of changing political and administrative systems.
site.historical_significance: Arslan Tash is important for studying political change along the Euphrates and the transformation of Aramean-associated centers under Assyrian rule. Its archaeological record should be read as a sequence of changing administrations.
site.major_findings: The site is represented by settlement and administrative remains, palace-related material, ivories, inscriptions, and evidence for the transition from Bit-Adini-associated political networks to Assyrian provincial administration.

locations.name: Elephantine
locations.description: Elephantine preserves papyri and settlement remains from a Persian-period community that used Aramaic for administration and daily affairs. It is included as an Aramaic archaeological context, not as an Aramean kingdom or a direct continuation of an Iron Age polity.

site.research_focus: Settlement archaeology, papyri, administration, religion, and Aramaic-speaking community life
site.excavation_history: Archaeological excavations and study of the island settlement have documented domestic, religious, and administrative contexts alongside the papyri. The current catalogue requires a dedicated campaign history and source bibliography for the fieldwork record.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a complete list of the archaeological teams and institutions responsible for the Elephantine excavations; those details remain pending source documentation.
site.description: Elephantine preserves papyri and settlement remains from a Persian-period community that used Aramaic for administration and daily affairs. It is included as an Aramaic archaeological context, not as an Aramean kingdom or a direct continuation of an Iron Age polity.
site.historical_significance: Elephantine is a key site for studying Imperial Aramaic and the daily life of an Aramaic-using community within the Persian Empire. It should not be presented as an Iron Age Aramean political center.
site.major_findings: The archaeological record includes settlement remains, religious contexts, and a major corpus of Aramaic papyri concerning administration, law, religion, and daily life under Achaemenid rule.

locations.name: Tayma Oasis
locations.description: Tayma was an oasis settlement with evidence for long-distance political and commercial connections. Aramaic inscriptions from the Persian period document the language’s use in northwestern Arabia without establishing an Aramean political identity for the oasis.

site.research_focus: Oasis settlement, inscriptions, long-distance exchange, and Achaemenid-period administration
site.excavation_history: Archaeological excavations, surveys, and conservation work at Tayma have investigated the oasis settlement, its inscriptions, architecture, and long-distance connections. The catalogue does not yet contain a complete campaign history or project bibliography.
site.excavation_team: The current catalogue does not yet provide a complete list of the archaeological teams and institutions working at Tayma; this information remains pending source documentation.
site.description: Tayma was an oasis settlement with evidence for long-distance political and commercial connections. Aramaic inscriptions from the Persian period document the language’s use in northwestern Arabia without establishing an Aramean political identity for the oasis.
site.historical_significance: Tayma demonstrates the wide geographic use of Aramaic in the Achaemenid period. Its evidence belongs to an oasis and administrative context rather than to an Aramean kingdom.
site.major_findings: Investigated evidence includes settlement remains, inscriptions, architectural contexts, and material connected with the oasis’s political and commercial networks during the Persian period.

locations.name: El-Maakir / Qaryat al-Kaafa
locations.description: El-Maakir / Qaryat al-Kaafa is recorded here as the reported provenance of an early anthropomorphic sandstone stele displayed in the Roads of Arabia exhibition. The catalogue follows the provenance given by the Wikimedia image record and does not infer a more precise archaeological context.

locations.name: Najran
locations.associated_context: Late antique Syriac Christian community in southern Arabia
locations.description: Najran was a major center of Syriac (Miaphysite) Christianity in southern Arabia during the 5th and 6th centuries AD. Its history should be reconstructed through late antique textual, ecclesiastical, and regional evidence; the location record does not by itself establish that every inhabitant shared one language or identity.

locations.name: Tel Dan
locations.description: Tel Dan is included as a location because the archaeology catalogue records the Tel Dan Stele there. The related evidence record provides the detailed inscription and historical context.

site.research_focus: Gate complex, cultic area, settlement layers, and the Tel Dan Stele
site.excavation_history: Systematic excavations began in 1966 under Avraham Biran of the Hebrew Union College/Nelson Glueck School of Biblical Archaeology and continued for decades. In 1993, Gila Cook, a member of Biran’s team, discovered the first fragment of the Tel Dan Stele; two additional fragments were found in 1994.
site.excavation_team: The principal long-term project was directed by Avraham Biran and involved the Nelson Glueck School of Biblical Archaeology, field archaeologists, architects, epigraphers, and specialists in the site’s artefacts and environmental evidence. Gila Cook made the initial 1993 stele discovery during the excavation.
site.description: Tel Dan preserves successive settlement layers, monumental gates, fortifications, a cultic area, and evidence for the city’s changing political connections. The site is also the findspot of the Tel Dan Stele, an Aramaic royal inscription recovered from a secondary architectural context.
site.historical_significance: Tel Dan connects archaeology, Aramaic epigraphy, and the political history of the southern Levant. The inscription is important evidence, but its wording, historical referent, and relationship to biblical narratives require careful source criticism.
site.major_findings: Excavations revealed the Iron Age gate complex, cultic installations, settlement layers, architectural remains, and the Tel Dan Stele. The stele is written in Aramaic and is significant for the history of Levantine kingdoms and the discussion of the phrase commonly read as ‘House of David’; its fragments were found reused in a later wall rather than in their original setting.
